reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Typically causes chronic occult gastrointestinal blood loss with iron-deficiency anaemia, and sometimes overt but usually slow bleeding
At endoscopy the classic appearance is red, stripe-like columns of ectatic vessels radiating from the pylorus across the antrum, resembling a watermelon
A diffuse punctate or honeycomb pattern is more common in patients with portal hypertension
Associations include cirrhosis and portal hypertension, connective-tissue diseases such as systemic sclerosis, chronic kidney disease and autoimmune conditions
It must be distinguished from portal hypertensive gastropathy, as the two have different distributions and treatments even though both may occur in cirrhosis
Biopsy, if taken, shows dilated mucosal capillaries with fibrin thrombi and fibromuscular hyperplasia of the lamina propria
First-line treatment is endoscopic ablation for GAVE, commonly with argon plasma coagulation, alongside iron replacement and transfusion as needed
reference.pathophysiology: Gastric antral vascular ectasia is characterised by dilated, tortuous mucosal capillaries and venules in the gastric antrum, often with fibrin thrombi, fibromuscular hyperplasia and spindle-cell proliferation in the lamina propria. The fragile ectatic vessels bleed easily, producing chronic slow blood loss and iron-deficiency anaemia. The precise cause is unclear but mechanical stress from antral peristalsis and prolapse, together with humoral and vasoactive factors, is thought to promote the vascular changes; it is frequently associated with cirrhosis, systemic sclerosis, chronic kidney disease and other systemic disorders. Importantly it is a distinct entity from portal hypertensive gastropathy despite overlapping in patients with liver disease.
additionalDifferentials: Gastric angiodysplasia and other vascular malformations
additionalInvestigations: Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy to identify the characteristic antral vascular pattern
Full blood count and iron studies to quantify anaemia and deficiency
Targeted biopsy where the diagnosis is uncertain
Assessment for underlying cirrhosis, portal hypertension and connective-tissue disease
Faecal occult blood testing and, if bleeding source unclear, further luminal investigation
redFlags: Failure to respond to endoscopic therapy, suggesting a need to reassess the diagnosis
Features of decompensated liver disease complicating management
reference.prognosis: Bleeding often responds to endoscopic ablation, though repeated sessions are commonly needed and recurrence is frequent; overall outcome is strongly influenced by any underlying disease such as cirrhosis.
pitfalls: Confusing it with portal hypertensive gastropathy and mismanaging treatment
Attributing iron-deficiency anaemia to other causes and overlooking the antral lesion
Expecting a single ablation session to be curative
Neglecting iron replacement while focusing only on endoscopic therapy
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
management: Endoscopic ablation, most commonly argon plasma coagulation, is first-line and usually needs repeated sessions
Use endoscopic band ligation or radiofrequency ablation for lesions refractory to argon plasma coagulation
Correct iron-deficiency anaemia with iron replacement and transfusion as required
Reserve surgical antrectomy for bleeding refractory to endoscopic therapy
Distinguish it from portal hypertensive gastropathy, since portal-pressure-lowering measures do not control the bleeding
Manage associated systemic disease such as cirrhosis, systemic sclerosis and chronic kidney disease
Provide endoscopic surveillance for recurrent bleeding given the high recurrence rate
